rationale: Cinnamon-containing cake was followed by a palatal blister and severe local pain after rupture. The exact spice, co-ingredients and diagnosis were unconfirmed. A single contact reaction supplies safety context with an unresolved Parkinson pain estimate.

Cinnamon-flavored mints were associated with oral burning and lesions. Withdrawal and re-use reproduced lesion changes. The challenge concerns the complete mint product, with ground cinnamon exposure and Parkinson pain outside its scope.
Among three selected intermittent burning cases patch tested for additives, one tested positive to cinnamon. The dietary advice outcomes were not linked to the cinnamon-positive patient.

A series of selected cinnamon-flavored oral product reactions reported burning in most cases. Clinical course is described for gum exposure and does not directly inform ground spice or Parkinson pain.

Cinnamon gum and candy were associated with localized contact lesions in a selected case series. The inaccessible symptoms table leaves pain and burning counts unverified. The 40 published cases are a separate literature review.
